title: New to faith, or coming back
subtitle: Twelve short sessions for someone who has just come to faith, or is coming back to the start: who Jesus is, how to read and pray, the church, and what to do when you fail or doubt.
intro: This track is for an adult who has just begun to follow Jesus, or who is coming back after years away and wants to start again from the beginning. It has twelve sessions. Each one takes about ten minutes, and you can take them a day apart or a week apart. Nothing here is timed, and nothing counts the days you miss.

Every session works the same way. You read a few short paragraphs, then open one page or tool on this site and use it, then come back. At the end there's one question to answer, one thing to do, and one verse to keep. If you can, go through it with one other person. Each session has a guide for a group at the bottom.

sessions.title: Who Jesus is
teaching: The Christian faith begins with a person. Before it asks anything of you, it asks you to look at Jesus, and the plainest way to do that is to read a Gospel for yourself. Mark is the shortest of the four, and he wastes no time. In his first chapter Jesus is baptized, calls four fishermen to follow him, drives out an unclean spirit, heals the sick, and touches a man with leprosy whom everyone else kept at a distance. The crowd is left asking, “What is this? A new teaching with authority!” (Mark 1:27).

Mark has already told you the answer in his first line, where he calls Jesus the Christ, the Son of God. Christians confess that Jesus is fully God and fully man in one person. That sentence took the church centuries to say with care, and you don't have to master it this week. Start where the first followers started, by watching what he does and listening to what he says. His first words in Mark ask for two things: repent, which means turn around, and believe, which means trust the news.

open.label: Mark 1, passage by passage
open.why: Mark is the shortest Gospel, and here each passage of his first chapter is explained in plain words under the text.

also.label: Who Jesus is
also.why: Seven short pictures of who Christians confess Jesus to be, and the question he asked his friends.

also.label: Mark 2, passage by passage

sessions.question: Which moment in Mark 1 would you most like to have seen, and what does it tell you about who Jesus is?
sessions.do: Read Mark 2 and Mark 3 before the next session, a chapter at a sitting, with the plain-words notes open under the text. Write down one thing Jesus says or does that surprises you.

verse.text: “The time is fulfilled,” He said, “and the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe in the gospel!”

group.open: When you first heard about Jesus, what did you think he was like?
discuss: In Mark 1, who seems to know who Jesus is, and who is still asking?
Jesus calls four fishermen and they leave their nets at once. What would have made that hard for them?
Jesus touches the man with leprosy before he heals him. What does that show you about Jesus?
group.pray: Thank God in your own words for one thing you saw in Jesus in this chapter, and ask him to help each person in the group see Jesus more clearly this week.

sessions.title: Why he died and rose
teaching: Every Gospel slows down when it reaches the last week of Jesus' life, because the writers knew it was the centre of the story. Jesus was crucified under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate. Christians confess that he died for us, and the Bible reaches for more than one picture to say how: a lamb at Passover, a ransom that sets a prisoner free, a servant who carries what others deserved, a victory over death itself. No one picture says it all. What they share is that God himself acted, out of love. The earliest summary of the faith puts it in one line: “Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3).

And the cross is not the end of the story. Christians confess that on the third day God raised Jesus in his body, the same body that had been buried, now made new. Paul says plainly that everything rests on it: if Christ has not been raised, faith is futile. Because he was raised, the forgiveness won at the cross is sealed, and death is not the final word over anyone who belongs to him. The resurrection does not take away grief. It gives grief a hope.

open.label: Why did Jesus die?
open.why: It sets out six pictures the Bible itself uses for what the cross did, held together, without choosing one over the rest.

also.label: The resurrection
also.why: What Christians believe happened on the third day, and why it matters, in seven pictures.

also.label: Did the resurrection actually happen?
also.why: Christians say their faith stands or falls on this event, so it is the claim to test.

sessions.question: Which of the Bible's pictures of the cross is easiest for you to take in, and which is hardest?
sessions.do: Read Mark 15 and Mark 16 in one sitting, slowly, as if you had never heard how it ends. Then tell one person what you read.

verse.text: But God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What did you think the cross was about before you began to read the Bible for yourself?
discuss: The film shows six pictures of what the cross did. Which one was new to you?
Paul says God proves his love at the cross. How is that different from a God who has to be talked into loving people?
Why do you think Paul stakes everything on the resurrection being a real event, and not only a teaching?
group.pray: Give thanks, each in a sentence or two, for what Jesus did, and pray by name for anyone in the group who is grieving or afraid of death.

sessions.title: Trusting him: grace and faith
teaching: Most people assume that religion is a ladder: be good enough, try harder, earn your way up. The Bible says plainly that the gap is too wide for that, and then it says something better. God crossed the gap from his own side. Paul writes, “For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast” (Ephesians 2:8-9). Grace is the free and undeserved favor of God. That is hard news for anyone who likes to earn things, and good news for anyone who knows they cannot.

Faith is how the gift is received. It isn't a work that pays for anything. It is empty hands taking what is given, which means trusting Jesus himself and resting on what he has done, and not on your own record. Then Paul adds a line people often miss: we are “created in Christ Jesus to do good works” (Ephesians 2:10). The good works come after. You are not saved by them, but you are saved for them. Churches describe the link between faith and works in different words, and the notes on this chapter set those out without choosing. On the gift itself they speak together.

open.label: Ephesians 2, passage by passage
open.why: Paul tells every Christian's story in ten verses: where we were, what God did, and what it means.

also.label: How salvation works
also.why: The same good news in nine pictures, from the first gift to the gift received.

also.label: What is grace? (the family catechism)
also.why: The catechism answers what grace, faith and repentance are in one sentence each.

sessions.question: Where do you still act as if God's love has to be earned?
sessions.do: Read Ephesians 2:1-10 aloud once a day for three days. On the third day, write one sentence that says in your own words what God has done.

verse.text: For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast.

group.open: What is the best gift anyone ever gave you that you could never repay?
discuss: Paul says the rescue had to be God's from start to finish. Why does that matter so much to him?
What is the difference between working for God's love and working because you already have it?
Verse 10 says God prepared good works for his people. What might one of those look like for you this week?
group.pray: Thank God for the gift in plain words, and ask him to show each person one place where they are still trying to earn what has already been given.

sessions.title: How to read the Bible
teaching: The Bible is a library of sixty-six books written over many centuries, and it tells one story: how God made us, how we went wrong, and how Jesus came to save us. Nobody understands all of it at once, and nobody is asked to. Begin with a Gospel, and read a whole chapter before you ask what any one verse means. Go slowly, and let it say what it says. Then ask the questions a careful reader asks of any page: who is speaking, to whom, what comes back again, and what surprises you.

You will meet parts you don't follow yet. That is normal, and it isn't a sign that you are reading badly. The Study Bible on this site puts notes beside every chapter, and for many chapters it explains each passage in plain words. A good habit for a new reader is one chapter a day of the Gospel of John, which takes three weeks. Short and steady is better than long and rare. The psalmist calls God's word a lamp, and a lamp lights the next few steps, which is as much as you need today.

open.label: How to study the Bible
open.why: Seven steps that work on any chapter. Learn them there, then try them on a real one.

also.label: The guided study of John 3
also.why: The same seven steps on one chapter, one screen at a time. It keeps your place if you stop.

also.label: Open John in the Study Bible
also.why: John has twenty-one chapters, so a chapter a day takes three weeks, with notes on every one of them.

sessions.question: What has kept you from reading the Bible before now, and what would make a chapter a day possible?
sessions.do: Choose a time and a place for reading, and tell one person what you chose. Then read John 1 today with the notes beside it.

verse.text: Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.

group.open: What is one book, of any kind, that you have read more than once, and why?
discuss: Which of the seven steps do you already do without thinking, and which is new to you?
Read John 3:1-8 aloud together. Who is speaking, who is listening, and what surprises you?
What do you do when you reach a part of the Bible you can't make sense of?
group.pray: Ask God, in your own words, to make each person hungry to read, and pray for the time and the place each one has chosen.

sessions.title: How to pray
teaching: Prayer is talking with God, who is our Father. You bring him worship, thanks, confession and requests, and you trust that he hears because of Jesus. It isn't a way of getting things out of God, and it doesn't depend on finding the right words. When his disciples asked him to teach them, Jesus gave them a pattern that Christians all over the world still pray. It begins, “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name” (Matthew 6:9).

If nobody ever taught you how to pray, begin with five minutes a day. Say the Lord's Prayer slowly, one line at a time, and stop where a line catches on something in your own life. Then borrow a psalm. The psalms are full of praise and thanks, and they are just as full of people asking God how long their trouble will last. Some prayers are not answered the way we longed for, and that hurts. The Bible doesn't hide it, and it doesn't say that it happens because of too little faith.

sessions.question: Which is hardest for you: thanking, asking, saying sorry, or waiting?
sessions.do: Set aside five minutes a day this week. Pray the Lord's Prayer slowly, then tell God one thing you are thankful for and one thing you need.

verse.text: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.

sessions.title: The Holy Spirit
teaching: The Holy Spirit is God himself, the third person of the Trinity, living in his people. He is neither a force nor a feeling. Christians agree that the Spirit gives new life, lives in every believer, and joins each one to Christ. Jesus' own picture is a vine and its branches: the branch lives because it is joined to the vine. Paul adds a family picture. Those who belong to Christ have been adopted, and “The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God’s children” (Romans 8:16).

The Spirit also changes people, and he does it slowly. Paul names nine kinds of fruit, beginning with love, joy and peace, and fruit takes a season to grow, so don't measure yourself after a week. The Spirit gives gifts as well, to each believer, for the good of all. Churches differ on whether some gifts, such as tongues, prophecy and healing, continue as they did in Acts, and on whether the baptism of the Spirit is a distinct experience after a person first believes. Your own church can tell you how it reads those passages. All of them confess that the Spirit is help for the weak, and never a reward for the strong.

open.label: The Holy Spirit in a believer

verse.text: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.

sessions.title: The church, and why it matters
teaching: This faith was never meant to be lived alone. The church is the whole company of God's people, gathered by the Spirit around Christ, and a building is only where some of them meet. God saves people into a family. Paul's picture is a body with many parts, where no part can say it does not need the others. The first Christians in Jerusalem “devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer” (Acts 2:42), and Christians still gather for the same four things.

So look for a faithful church, which isn't the same thing as a perfect one, and go more than once before you decide. Look first for a church where the Scriptures are preached as true and the gospel of grace is clear. Then stay long enough to be known. Some people hear all this with a knot in the stomach, because a church is where they were hurt. If that is you, it matters, and nobody here will hurry you past it. There's a page on this site written for people hurt by a church, and it's worth reading before you visit anywhere.

sessions.title: Baptism and the Lord's Supper
teaching: Jesus gave his church two things to do with ordinary stuff: water, and a meal of bread and a cup. His last command to his disciples included baptism, in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. On the night he was betrayed he took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and told his friends to do this in remembrance of him. Both signs point away from the person taking part and toward what Jesus did at the cross and the empty tomb. Paul sums up what holds Christians together in a few words: “one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4:5).

Churches share those commands, and they differ on some of what follows. Some baptize the children of believers, and others baptize only those who confess faith for themselves. Some pour or sprinkle water, and others take a person under it and up again. Churches also describe in different words what baptism does and what happens in the Supper. Faithful Christians have read the same chapters with care and landed in different places, and this track doesn't choose between them. If you haven't been baptized, or you aren't sure whether to come to the Lord's Supper, ask your pastor how your church practices both, and why.

group.pray: Thank God for the two signs Jesus gave, and pray for anyone in the group who is thinking about baptism or about coming to the Lord's Supper.

sessions.title: When you fail
teaching: You will fail. Sometimes it will be an old habit that comes back, and sometimes a new wrong you didn't think you were capable of. The question that follows is a heavy one: has God turned away? John wrote to Christians, and he assumed they would need this sentence: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). To confess is to agree with God about your sin, to call it what he calls it. The way out isn't to deny it, and it isn't to despair over it. It is to bring it into the light.

Notice the two words John chooses. Faithful means God keeps his word. Just is more surprising, because you might expect a just God to punish. But God's forgiveness rests on the cross, and not on pretending that sin is small. Grace does not make sin small, and sin does not make grace run out. In the story Jesus told, the father sees his son far off and runs to him before the son can finish his speech. So when you fail, don't hide, and don't wait until you feel clean enough. Confess it to God, turn from it, and where you have wronged someone, go and put it right.

sessions.title: When you doubt
teaching: Having questions doesn't mean your faith was never real. The Bible shows people who believed and struggled at once, and it tells the church to “have mercy on those who doubt” (Jude 22). A father once brought his suffering son to Jesus and cried out, “I do believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24). Jesus did not send him away to get his certainty in order first. He helped the boy.

So don't bury a doubt, and don't feed it in secret either. Say it to God, and then to a Christian you trust. Then look for the question in its strongest form and for the strongest answer, because a doubt is easier to weigh once it has been stated plainly. This site was built with that in mind. The Honest Answers take the hard questions one at a time, and the longer library called the case for the faith puts each objection at full strength before it replies. Christianity makes claims about real events, above all that Jesus rose, and it tells you where to check.

open.label: What if Christianity is wrong?
open.why: It puts the case against believing at full strength before it answers, which is what an honest question is owed.

also.label: The empty tomb

sessions.question: What is the question about the faith you would most like answered, and who could you ask?
sessions.do: Write your hardest question down in one sentence. Then look for it among the Honest Answers or in the case for the faith, read what is there, and note where you would push back.

verse.text: Immediately the boy’s father cried out, “I do believe; help my unbelief!”

care: If you are a person whose conscience never rests, who keeps checking whether you have really believed, hear John's words: “Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things” (1 John 3:20). Such fear can be part of anxiety or a habit of the mind, and that is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust, and if the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.pray: Invite each person to name one doubt or question before God without anyone answering it, then ask God together for mercy and for light.

sessions.title: Living it on a Tuesday
teaching: Faith is lived on ordinary days. Most of following Jesus happens at work, at a kitchen table, in traffic, and in the way you speak to the person who irritates you. The Bible has a great deal to say about those places: money, anger, work, rest, marriage, friendship, worry. Paul's rule covers all of it: “And whatever you do, in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through Him” (Colossians 3:17).

That can sound like a demand to fix everything by Friday. It isn't. Take one thing. Ask what you are facing this week, find what Scripture says about it, and do the next faithful thing in that one place. Wisdom in the Bible is seldom a rule for every case. It is a way of seeing your situation with God in it, and it is learned slowly, mostly by practice, and often in the company of people further along than you. Good works don't earn God's love. They are what a life looks like when it already has it.

sessions.title: What next
teaching: Twelve sessions don't make anyone a finished Christian, and no one becomes one in this life. What you have now is a start. You have looked at Jesus, heard the good news of the cross and the empty tomb, and begun to read, to pray, and to gather with his people. Paul wrote to a young church that he was sure of one thing: “He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus” (Philippians 1:6). The work is God's, and he is patient with it.

So keep going in small, steady ways. Stay in a Gospel until you finish it. Keep the five minutes of prayer. Belong to a church, and let a few people there know you well enough to ask how you really are. Then choose one next thing, and only one. The eight-week plan for a new Christian takes these same beginnings further, a week at a time. The study guide lets you go over the first steps with a friend or a pastor. And when you have finished Mark, you can read it again more slowly, a chapter at a time.
